newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia coffee higher, London seen sliding.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia coffee higher, London seen sliding.

text.p: Indonesian robusta coffee prices were higher on Monday on supply concerns despite sharp falls in London and New York futures last Friday, traders said.

Grade four robusta was quoted at 4,700-4,850 rupiah/kg in the key growing region of Lampung in South Sumatra, compared with 4,250-4,300 rupiah last week. The export price was quoted at $1,950 FOB Lampung against $1,830-$1,850 a week ago.

Traders said some investors forecast London's benchmark July contract will plunge by as much as $400 on paper when the market opens later on Monday. However, they said a decline of about $200 was more likely.
London's July robusta contract closed $135 down at $2,465/tonne on Friday in a correction to Thursday's scorching rally to a 20-month high on long liquidation coupled with pre-weekend profit-taking.
Later that day, New York's July arabica contract tumbled 38.40 cents to close at 276.40 cents/lb after an explosive three-day rally that took prices to a 20-year peak.

"Local (Indonesian) prices were not affected by Friday's falls in London and New York because supply is getting tight," one trader said. "Between 50 and 60 percent of the crop has been done, and supply will be really tight from June."

"My estimate is that traders are holding 20 percent of the crop while farmers are holding another 20 percent," he said. "Getting beans after June or July will be tough. Local prices are relatively high because of this reason."
Another trader said he expected domestic values to come under pressure if London robusta futures continue their decline from last Friday.
"There's not much activity in the local market today because players are watching London. If prices there continue to fall, we will see some decline in local prices as well," he said.

The traders said coffee growers had mixed feelings about the current market situation because while relatively high domestic prices were boosting their incomes, the shortfall in production was limiting sales.
"Some farmers are seeing shortfalls of up to 40 percent," one trader said. "With almost half of his crop gone because of bad weather, he is making much less from this price rally."
He said exporters were also feeling the pinch because they had to pay a relatively high price for their local beans.
"Furthermore, they have to take the risks involved in such a situation, when prices can come crashing down," he added.
The traders said they had not yet heard of any defaults in coffee contracts since the price rally.
"I have not heard of any defaults yet," one trader said. "Everybody has been honouring his contracts and I don't think it will happen for robusta."
The traders said sellers defaulted on some contracts for arabica because prices had soared since they signed.
But they said the contracts involved did not amount to more than 100 tonnes for the higher-priced arabicas.
